items.title: RobPiCFM: A Training-Free Target-Conditioned Method with Foundation Models for Robotic Picking in Clutter
items.abstract: Picking objects from clutter remains a challenging problem in robotic manipulation, as it requires connecting object-level perception, grasp generation, collision-aware selection, and robot motion execution in unstructured scenes. In this paper, we present RobPiCFM, an open-source, trainingfree method for target-conditioned picking in cluttered scenes. The proposed method combines pretrained foundation-modelbased perception with RGB-D geometry, 6D object pose estimation and tracking, grasp candidate generation, constraintbased grasp filtering, and motion planning. Unlike end-toend manipulation policies, the method does not require taskspecific policy learning and relies instead on pretrained visual models and explicit robot execution constraints. We evaluate the method on a real robotic setup in a cluttered tabletop scenario using objects with different shapes and grasping properties. The ablation study shows that the proposed grasp filtering mechanism increases the normalized task score from 16.7 to 53.1, while target pre-segmentation further improves the score to 60.6. https://github.com/Dorian-BAUDU/RobPiCFM.git

items.title: Written, Not Trained: LLM-Written Stack Machines Proven Correct at Every Length
items.abstract: Stack- and tape-augmented recurrent networks were made differentiable so that they could be trained, yet on the Chomsky-hierarchy benchmark of Delétang et al. they rarely extrapolate exactly beyond the training lengths. We hand the hard version of the machine to a large language model (LLM). R0S is a recurrent controller with Heaviside units, ternary weights and integer biases that drives an unbounded discrete stack through argmax push, pop and no-op actions. From a plain-language specification and without running the network, Claude Opus wrote R0S networks for five benchmark tasks and Dyck-2; all 30 attempts pass our scorer. Two mechanical methods, a grammar-summary fixpoint and a lockstep product with a reference pushdown automaton, prove all 25 networks on five tasks correct on every input the task generator produces, at every length; the 5 bucket-sort networks pass the scorer but are wrong, because they count with bounded counters. On modular arithmetic and equation solving the proven networks have 185–591 non-zero parameters.Learning from input-output examples finds no exact network there: straight-through training of R0S itself (20,000 steps, 4 learning-rate and initialisation arms) is exact in 0 of 120 runs and Delétang's four differentiable models in 0 of 120 runs; in a near-full version of their training setting on modular arithmetic, 0 of 180 runs are exact, although the best Stack-RNN reaches a Delétang score (accuracy averaged over lengths 41–500) of 95.1 (theirs: 96.1).Placed behind a 16k-parameter interface inside a frozen Qwen3.5-0.8B, with a read-in trained per token on the generator's labels, the proven modular-arithmetic network answers correctly at all 14 tested lengths from 5 to 500 (0 errors on 4,500 test-length inputs, in each of 3 seeds); the same interface around the trained Stack-RNN reaches 88.4% exact match at length 500, and LoRA fine-tuning without a module, trained on answers only, falls to the majority-answer rate. We do not claim that stack networks are untrainable in general, or that the interface can be learned from answers alone
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Simulation of Entanglement between Two AIs: A Proof of Concept for Ontology Matching
items.abstract: This paper proposes a computational simulation of the concept of entanglement between two artificial agents, applied as a proof of concept for ontology matching. The simulation, to be developed in a future implementation stage, will instantiate two independent AI agents, each representing one of the two ontologies to be matched, and each operating in its own private reference frame generated by orthogonal random matrices with distinct seeds. Because the two reference frames are incommensurable, the agents are, by construction, uncorrelated: the expected cosine similarity between any pair of representations is zero. A linear channel (ridge regression codec) will then be trained on a small set of known correspondence pairs, analogous to calibration pairs, and is expected to align the two reference frames on held-out pairs, while a randomized control set should remain at noise level. We formalize this setup through a diagnosis protocol that will report (i) the alignment residual against the theoretical optimal frame matcher, (ii) the cosine similarity before and after the channel, and (iii) the gap between correlated pairs and a random control. The proof of concept will be carried out on the Anatomy track of the OAEI, using its public gold standard, in order to demonstrate methodological feasibility. The intended result is a reproducible, locally executable demonstration that learning a mapping between two agents' representations is mathematically equivalent to concentrating correlation on a low-dimensional subspace, the computational analogue of partial entanglement, and that this learned channel can support automated ontology matching. The program is still under development and will be made available upon completion.
